'''R. David Britt''' is the Winston Ko Chair and Distinguished Professor of Chemistry at the [[University of California, Davis]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Oskin|first=Becky|date=2018-05-30|title=R. David Britt Named as Winston Ko Professor in Science Leadership|url=https://lettersandscience.ucdavis.edu/news/r-david-britt-named-winston-ko-professor-science-leadership|access-date=2021-05-23|website=UC Davis College of Letters and Science|language=en}}</ref> Britt uses [[electron paramagnetic resonance]] (EPR) spectroscopy to study [[Metalloprotein|metalloenzymes]] and enzymes containing [[Radical (chemistry)|organic radicals]] in their [[active site]]s.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|title=R. David Britt receives 2018 Zavoisky Award|url=https://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2018-09/kfu-rd092518.php|access-date=2021-05-23|website=EurekAlert!|language=en}}</ref> Britt is the recipient of multiple awards for his research, including the [[Bioinorganic Chemistry Award]] in 2019 and the Bruker Prize in 2015 from the Royal Society of Chemistry.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=2016-10-27|title=R. David Britt|url=https://chemistry.ucdavis.edu/people/david-britt|access-date=2021-05-23|website=Chemistry|language=en}}</ref> He has received a Gold Medal from the International EPR Society (2014), and the Zavoisky Award from the Kazan Scientific Center of the [[Russian Academy of Sciences]] (2018).<ref name=":2" /> He is a Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] and of the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]].<ref name=":0" />

== Early life and education ==
Britt studied at the North Carolina State University, graduating with his B.S. in physics in 1978.<ref name=":0" /> He completed his graduate studies in Physics at the University of California, Berkeley, graduating with his Ph.D. in 1988.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite thesis|title=Electron spin echo spectroscopy of photosynthesis|url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/303692298/A6434245B00D456BPQ|publisher=University of California, Berkeley|date=1988|place=United States – California|degree=Ph.D.|language=English|first=Ralph David|last=Britt}}</ref> At Berkeley, Britt worked in the laboratory of Prof. Melvin P. Klein as a [[NSF-GRFP|NSF Graduate Research Fellow]] on the construction of a [[pulsed electron paramagnetic resonance]] (EPR) spectrometer.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Britt|first1=R. David|last2=Zimmermann|first2=Jean Luc|last3=Sauer|first3=Kenneth|last4=Klein|first4=Melvin P.|date=1989|title=Ammonia binds to the catalytic manganese of the oxygen-evolving complex of photosystem II. Evidence by electron spin-echo envelope modulation spectroscopy|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/pdf/10.1021/ja00192a006|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=111|issue=10|pages=3522–3532|doi=10.1021/ja00192a006|bibcode=1989JAChS.111.3522B |issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Britt was able to use the electron [[spin echo]] envelope modulation (ESEEM) technique with this spectrometer to study the molecular structure of the manganese-containing [[oxygen-evolving complex]] (OEC).<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Britt|first1=R. David|last2=Sauer|first2=Kenneth|last3=Klein|first3=Melvin P.|last4=Knaff|first4=David B.|last5=Kriauciunas|first5=Aidas|last6=Yu|first6=Chang An|last7=Yu|first7=Linda|last8=Malkin|first8=Richard|date=1991-02-19|title=Electron spin echo envelope modulation spectroscopy supports the suggested coordination of two histidine ligands to the Rieske iron-sulfur centers of the cytochrome b6f complex on spinach and the cytochrome bc1 complexes of Rhodospirillum rubrum, Rhodobacter sphaeroides R-26, and bovine heart mitochondria|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/pdf/10.1021/bi00221a023|journal=Biochemistry|volume=30|issue=7|pages=1892–1901|doi=10.1021/bi00221a023|pmid=1847076|issn=0006-2960|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Citation|last1=Britt|first1=R. David|chapter=Pulsed EPR Studies of the Manganese Center of the Oxygen-Evolving Complex of Photosystem II|date=1990|chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-009-0511-5_176|title=Current Research in Photosynthesis: Proceedings of the VIIIth International Conference on Photosynthesis Stockholm, Sweden, August 6–11, 1989|pages=769–772|editor-last=Baltscheffsky|editor-first=M.|place=Dordrecht|publisher=Springer Netherlands|language=en|doi=10.1007/978-94-009-0511-5_176|isbn=978-94-009-0511-5|access-date=2021-05-23|last2=Derose|first2=Victoria J.|last3=Yachandra|first3=Vittal K.|last4=Kim|first4=Dennis H.|last5=Sauer|first5=Kenneth|last6=Klein|first6=Melvin P.|chapter-url-access=subscription}}</ref> Understanding of the OEC could improve our understanding of the mechanisms of the [[light-dependent reactions]] of [[photosynthesis]], and could lead to the development of [[artificial photosynthesis]].

== Independent career ==
Britt began his independent career at the University of California, Davis in 1989 as an assistant professor.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=R. David Britt CV|url=http://brittepr.ucdavis.edu/images/britt/rdbonepagecv.pdf}}</ref> He was promoted to associate professor in 1994, and to full professor in 1997.<ref name=":1" /> Since 2005, he has served as chair of the Department of Chemistry at Davis, and 2018 he was named the Winston Ko Professorship in Science Leadership.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" />

== Research ==
[[Electron paramagnetic resonance]] (EPR) spectroscopy is a technique that measures the relaxation of unpaired electron spins in an applied magnetic field. This technique is particularly useful for studying the mechanism of catalysis of metalloenzymes and enzymes containing organic radicals, as these mechanistic intermediates often contain unpaired electrons and thus give a distinct EPR signal. Enzymatic systems that the Britt group studies include the [[oxygen-evolving complex]] of [[photosystem II]],<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2012-11-01|title=Comparison of cobalt and manganese in the chemistry of water oxidation|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0010854512001099|journal=Coordination Chemistry Reviews|language=en|volume=256|issue=21–22|pages=2445–2452|doi=10.1016/j.ccr.2012.04.039|issn=0010-8545|last1=McAlpin|first1=J. Gregory|last2=Stich|first2=Troy A.|last3=Casey|first3=William H.|last4=Britt|first4=R. David|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Britt|first1=R. David|last2=Peloquin|first2=Jeffrey M.|last3=Campbell|first3=Kristy A.|date=2000|title=Pulsed and Parallel-Polarization EPR Characterization of the Photosystem II Oxygen-Evolving Complex|url=http://www.annualreviews.org/doi/10.1146/annurev.biophys.29.1.463|journal=Annual Review of Biophysics and Biomolecular Structure|language=en|volume=29|issue=1|pages=463–495|doi=10.1146/annurev.biophys.29.1.463|pmid=10940256|issn=1056-8700|url-access=subscription}}</ref> the H<sub>2</sub>-producing [[Hydrogenase|[FeFe] hydrogenases]],<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Britt|first1=R. David|date=2014-08-19|title=Paramagnetic Intermediates Generated by Radical S-Adenosylmethionine (SAM) Enzymes|url=https://doi.org/10.1021/ar400235n|journal=Accounts of Chemical Research|volume=47|issue=8|pages=2235–2243|doi=10.1021/ar400235n|issn=0001-4842|pmc=4139163|pmid=24991701}}</ref>

With then-postdoctoral scholar Stefan Stoll, Britt developed EasySpin, an [[Open-source software|open-source]] [[MATLAB]] software toolbox for simulating and fitting a wide range of EPR spectra.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Stoll|first1=Stefan|last2=Britt|first2=R.
